body:
Having discussed defaulted const generics with @varkor a tiny bit during the winter holidays, I thought I'd try to help with this PR.

(Note: we have extracted the parsing parts of this PR, and landed them in #80547. They were also fixed to use to existing "unstable syntax" mechanism, specifically in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/80547/commits/942b7ce2c14b1c4fde5b9f27aa5bef39e0b990d5. There are still parsing changes in this PR, eg in `ast_validation` and I feel like some are issues during rebasing, some are removed in later commits, and others could be subsumed by other WIP I had in https://github.com/lqd/rust/commits/more_const_generics_defaults about the ordering of params -- especially since the existing type generics parameters with defaults seem incorrectly ordered -- diagnostics, tests, and so on. I haven't had the time to open a PR for them yet, and they could have bitrotted, but who knows maybe some of those could be of interest to y'all)


> Alright so I've added a query, but expect_local inside of it breaks for external crates in the test I added, not sure how to fix that.

I wonder if this conclusion is still correct ? The error in the test doesn't look like a problem with the query, right ?

```
error[E0282]: type annotations needed for `Defaulted<{_: usize}>`
  --> /checkout/src/test/ui/const-generics/defaults/external.rs:12:13
   |
LL |     let v = Defaulted;
   |         -   ^^^^^^^^^ cannot infer the value of const parameter `N` declared on the struct `Defaulted`
```

[lcnr's test is different](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/75384#issuecomment-787890606), it has explicit constructors
```rust
impl ConstDefault {
    fn new() -> Self {
        ConstDefault
    }
}
```

AKA `ConstDefault::<3>::new()`

If you change your [external.rs](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/f2a44876a1e8fe6138a97ecf86fc865a2c4dfa1a/src/test/ui/const-generics/defaults/external.rs) test to make it local only, by removing the extern crate and `Defaulted` references, you should see that this part of the test

```rust
struct Local<const N: usize = 4>;

fn main() {
    let l = Local;
}
```

doesn't build either, and has the same errors as currently shown for the auxiliary crate.

If one changes both `Local` and `const_defaulty::Defaulted` to use the pattern shown in lcnr's test, this should work. That's why I feel like the query does work with external crate generics. 

(By "work", I mean everything up to codegen: a check-pass test should work, but not a run-pass IIUC: that is, I believe there's still something missing in the codegen; at least I can't link locally on windows: it almost seems as if the `Defaulted::new` call is using a different symbol than the definition, one with the default const generics parameter in the mangled name, the other without it.)

That being said, with the changes to the test I mentioned above to make the external crates test work with explicit constructors, I believe this PR would pass CI and contain at the very least some working tests: making it acceptable to land as-is as a first step ? (possibly after a final cleanup, and a last quick review pass by @varkor / @lcnr)

> huh... this regressed rustdoc?

that's pretty strange! i have no idea if 1% is meaningful in these tests though.

> It seems to have had no effect on any of the other tests

i'm assuming these are run with a release build, which statically disables all tracing, right? i didn't expect a performance improvement in that case --- i expected it in the case where tracing was _not_ statically disabled. the hope, specifically, was that performance would be improved enough that it wouldn't be necessary to disable tracing at compile time, so that it can be enabled in release builds just by setting `RUSTC_LOG` without recompiling, which @Mark-Simulacrum expressed interest in in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/74726#issuecomment-667254343.

body:
Currently we have `NonNull::as_ref` and `NonNull::as_mut` taking `&(mut) self` (both stabilized - sadly). Shall I also alter `as_uninit_slice` to take `&self` and returning `&[MaybeUninit]` and add `as_uninit_slice_mut`? Since `NonNull` implements `Copy` I don't like passing it as a reference, as you will almost never have a reference to `NonNull`, especially not a `&mut NonNull`.

This btw. also applies to `as_mut_ptr` which converts a slice to a non-slice pointer. On nightly there is `MaybeUninit::first_ptr(_mut)` which maybe could also be used on slice pointers instead. With this naming we could keep a single naming scheme.

body:
To do better, we'd have to either
* pass a span through the error machinery (i.e., add a `Span` field to `InterpError`) which (if present) overwrites the span of the topmost frame, or
* make it so that the frame knows it is currently evaluating a const, and can report its span.

In the light of [this chaos](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/71800#issuecomment-671805859), I am not sure I want to add yet another `Span` field to errors, and such "overwriting" behavior is often confusing. So if we think that we should try to do better, my proposal would be to replace this field of `Frame`
```rust
    pub loc: Option<mir::Location>,
```
by something of a type like `Result<mir::Location, Span>`, so that we can say what the span is when we are not currently evaluating a statement in that frame.
author: RalfJung

body: Yes, I also prefer that proposal. Although `Result` isn't the best type here, I'm not sure the situation warrants its own enum (though that could make it more obvious that something unusual is going on here). The current `None` situation could be represented by `Err(DUMMY_SP)`

author: davidtwco

body:
I'm... not sure about this. This is polymorphzing based on the `DefId`, which for some shims is always the same `DefId` (of something in libcore with a builtin impl), and some shims have some types in the `InstanceDef` computed from the `Substs`.

The ones I can think of that could work well are `ReifyShim` and `VtableShim`, as they are shims around a user function, rather than builtin implementation of something in libcore. There might also be one or two that are like this but for closures.

But either way we probably want an exhaustive match to decide whether to polymorphize.

body:
Ah, didn't realize there was a PR. So, as mentioned in the issue, you need to bless the tests (and add a new test for the case in the issue). The fastest way to do that is `./x.py test --stage 1 --bless src/test/ui --test-args min_const_fn`. That's a mouth full, but all of these flags actually do help:

* `--stage 1` just builds a compiler and runs the tests, without first checking whether you can still build a compiler with that new compiler
* `--bless` updates `.stderr` files, you may still need to touch the source files (e.g. the `//~ is unsafe` comment in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/c94ed5ca91f1363b66970ce2cbd6e2773e3cb1d3/src/test/ui/consts/min_const_fn/min_const_fn_unsafe_bad.rs#L1 should now probably be removed)
* `--test-args min_const_fn` only runs tests with `min_const_fn` in their name

author: CloudNClock

body:
You already have a merge commit in here, so please rebase on top of latest `origin/master` while also squashing:
```
git fetch origin
git rebase --interactive origin/master
```
That should not create any merge commits. See for example [this explanation](https://thoughtbot.com/blog/git-interactive-rebase-squash-amend-rewriting-history) of rebasing.

The reviewer will be notified when you do a regular push, but force-pushes unfortunately do not reliably trigger notifications (GitHub is acting rather strange there), so generally it is a good idea to ask the reviewer to have another look when the PR is ready again.

Updated with the apple exception.

@pietroalbini Do you have ideas on how that would work?  I had thought about moving to some kind of structured format (like it used to be), but it didn't seem to really improve things.

The concern with computing it is that the data needs to reside somewhere.  The tier status doesn't exist anywhere else, and I would be reluctant to add it to the spec definition.  Whether or not host and std vs no_std is only encoded through various shell scripts in the CI directory, and I don't think that's really parseable. And the "notes" section would need to go somewhere.

One idea I had was to query the rustup manifest to at least check the host and std status, but that would need to be done outside of regular CI runs since the publish happens separately.  One possibility is to set up a scheduled task (like once a day) that could query it and then send an alert if something is off (email? issue? zulip?).  However, that would only be useful for targets that change their status, and that is extremely rare AFAIK.

body:
> Is this what you meant with using `FromStr`?

It's close to what I had in mind. There are a couple of design possibilities here. Your code currently panics on IO errors, something we certainly don't want. We could:
- Create a new error type `enum InputError<P: FromStr> { Io(io::Error), Parse(P::Err) }` and return that
- Return a parse error as an IO error with `ErrorKind::InvalidInput` (however, that would add a `Error + Send + Sync` bound to `T::Err` ... adding to the already large function signature)

I'm not a fan of the two macro based possibilities you posted. Macros in general *could* be a path forward, though. 

---

I am still kind of waiting for input on how to proceed with this PR. *Maybe* I will find the time to write a summary about all possible API designs I can think of, but I won't promise.
author: LukasKalbertodt

body:
I found some time and wrote a couple of things about "prior art", including other languages and Rust crates. This PR is probably not the best place to put it, but I figured it could help in this whole discussion. If there is a bug in my comment, or something can be improved, or I should add something: please tell me (or directly edit this comment if you have the GitHub privileges). --- ## Prior art (stdout flushing is ignored in all examples) ### In other languages (I am by no means an expert in all these languages. I just picked what I thought was "the main way" to read values from stdin. Mostly by googling "{lang} guessing game".) #### C: `scanf` ```c printf("Your guess: "); int guess; scanf("%d", &i); ``` #### C++: iostreams ```cpp cout << "Your guess: "; int guess; cin >> guess; ``` #### Java: `Scanner` ```java Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in); System.out.print("Your guess: "); input.nextInt(); ``` #### JavaScript (Node) ```javascript const rl = readline.createInterface({ input: process.stdin, output: process.stdout }); rl.question('Your guess: ', (answer) => { const guess = parseInt(answer); rl.close(); }); ``` (Note though that JS has far better ways for programming beginners to get user input: through the browser. Reading from stdin easily is probably not that much of a priority.) #### Python: `input` ```python guess = int(input("Your guess: ")) ``` #### Ruby ```ruby puts "Enter guess: " guess = gets.chomp.to_i ``` (Technically not better than Rust as you have to do everything manually, but it's very short so I included it here.) #### Not better than Rust I know this is somewhat subjective, but these are the language where I feel that their standard libraries or core languages don't offer a way to read values that is better than Rust's current API (prompt, read string, and parse yourself). - C#: `Console.Write`, `Console.ReadLine` and parsing - Go: - Haskell: `putStr`, `getLine`, `read`
### Rust libraries #### [`text_io`](https://docs.rs/text_io/0.1.8/text_io/) ```rust print!("Your guess: "); let guess: i32 = read!(); // or: let guess; scan!("{}", guess); ``` #### [`scan-rules`](https://docs.rs/scan-rules/0.2.0/scan_rules/index.html) ```rust print!("Your guess: "); let_readln!(let guess: u32); ``` #### [`scan_fmt`](https://docs.rs/scan_fmt/0.2.5/scan_fmt/) ```rust print!("Your guess: ") let (guess,) = scanln_fmt!("{}", u32)?; ``` ---
### Overview | | Can prompt | Can parse | Can match literal strings | Can read multiple values | | ------ | ---------- | --------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------ | | C: `scanf` | ✗ | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ | | C++: iostreams | ✗ | ✔ | ✗ | ✔ | | Java: `Scanner` | ✗ | ✔ |(✔)|(✔)| | JavaScript (Node) | ✔ | ✗ | ✗?|(✔)| | Python: `input` | ✔ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | | Ruby | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | | --- ||||| | crate: `text_io` | ✗ | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ | | crate: `scan_rules` | ✗ | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ | | crate: `scan_fmt` | ✗ | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ |

author: pickfire

body:
> Just wondering if it is reading as String will the compiler optimize it such that there are no parsing (zero-cost)?

What do you mean here? If input is derived from the user, then it has to be validated as UTF8 in order to use it in a String. "Zero-cost abstractions" means you still have to perform the minimum amount of work required.
author: workingjubilee

body:
> Just wondering if it is reading as `String` will the compiler optimize it such that there are no parsing (zero-cost)?

Yes, it would not be "parsed". See [the `FromStr` impl for `String`](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/fd702d2919fe23eeaf59574040d0b29853d44289/library/alloc/src/string.rs#L2151-L2157). It would basically clone the input string once though. Not sure if the compiler can optimize that sufficiently. 

> If input is derived from the user, then it has to be validated as UTF8 in order to use it in a String. 

Yes, that has to be done anyway if we want to use `FromStr`, as it's input is `&str`.

> If I am correct, if the user wants `String` they need do add the type `let s: String = input()?` 

Yes. Oftentimes though, the type is already specified somewhere and type inference would do the rest. Not to say that I am against having a function that always returns `String`.

> but if we remove `FromStr` logic from this, they could just `let s = input()?`, but if they want `FromStr` or digits, it is just one word away, `let d = input()?.parse().expect("digit")`, 

`input()?.parse()?` would still be very short, but it would require an error type that can be created from arbitrary errors. I would not be comfortable recommending `input().parse.expect("..")` though, as a panic is the wrong way to deal with that parse error. 

> I would say having an extra enum `InputError` probably would not play well with `?` for `io::Result<()>`.

I think I don't understand. How do you mean?

@rust-lang/lang, I propose to guarnatee for a bunch of types that `Option<T>` has the same size as `T`, and that `T` may be transmuted to `Option<T>`.
